what_its_for: Ravulizumab-cwvz is used to treat certain serious blood and kidney conditions where your immune system mistakenly attacks your own red blood cells or kidneys. These conditions include paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS), generalized myasthenia gravis (a muscle weakness disease), and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD, a nerve disease affecting the eyes and spine). It works by blocking a part of your immune system called complement, which helps stop it from damaging your own cells.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it goes directly into your vein through a needle or catheter. A trained healthcare provider, nurse, or doctor will give you this infusion in a clinic, hospital, or infusion center. You should NOT try to give this medicine to yourself at home unless your doctor has specifically trained you and approved it. Each infusion takes about 1.5 to 4 hours depending on your dose. Before your first dose, you MUST receive a vaccine to protect against a serious bacterial infection called meningococcal disease (Neisseria meningitidis). If you cannot get vaccinated before starting, your doctor will put you on antibiotics to protect you until you can be vaccinated.
dosing: Your dose depends on your body weight and the condition being treated. Your doctor will calculate the right dose for you. Most adults receive a loading (starting) dose on Day 1, followed by maintenance doses given every 8 weeks. Children and teenagers may receive doses more or less frequently depending on their weight. Never try to adjust your dose on your own — always follow your doctor's instructions exactly.
missed_dose: It is very important not to miss your infusion appointments. If you miss a dose or need to reschedule, call your doctor or infusion center right away. Missing doses can cause your condition to get worse very quickly. If you stop this medicine suddenly, you are at high risk for serious complications, including dangerous blood clots, kidney failure, or severe worsening of your symptoms. Never stop treatment without talking to your doctor first.
storage: This medicine is stored and handled by healthcare professionals. The vials are kept refrigerated at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). They should be protected from light and should NOT be frozen or shaken. Once prepared for infusion, the diluted solution should be used promptly. You do not need to worry about storing this medication at home.
what_to_avoid: Avoid skipping or delaying your scheduled infusion appointments. Avoid exposure to people who are sick, especially with bacterial infections, as this medicine weakens part of your immune system and makes you more vulnerable to certain serious infections. Avoid stopping this medication suddenly without your doctor's guidance. Tell all of your doctors and dentists that you are on this medicine before any procedures or surgeries.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor immediately or go to the emergency room if you experience: a severe headache, stiff neck, fever, sensitivity to light, confusion, or a skin rash — these can be signs of a life-threatening bacterial meningitis infection. Also seek help right away for: chest pain, difficulty breathing, sudden swelling of the face or throat, signs of a blood clot (such as leg pain, redness, or swelling), dark or cola-colored urine, sudden decrease in urination, extreme fatigue, or yellowing of your skin or eyes. Always carry the Safety Card provided by your doctor so emergency healthcare providers know you are on this medicine.
when_it_works: Some patients begin to feel improvements within the first few weeks of starting treatment, but the full benefit may take longer — sometimes several months. Your doctor will monitor your blood tests regularly to check how well the medicine is working. It is important to keep all of your follow-up appointments even if you feel better.
special_populations: Children and Teenagers: Ravulizumab-cwvz can be used in children and adolescents for certain conditions. Doses are carefully calculated based on body weight. Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The effects of this medicine on an unborn baby or nursing infant are not fully known, so your doctor will carefully weigh the risks and benefits with you. Older Adults: Older patients can use this medicine, but your doctor will monitor you closely. Kidney or Liver Problems: Dose adjustments are generally not required, but your doctor will monitor your condition carefully. Meningococcal Risk in All Patients: Regardless of age, ALL patients must be vaccinated against meningococcal bacteria before or shortly after starting this medicine.
